U.S. and European credit markets 
In U.S. and European credit markets, credit spreads on both investment-grade bonds and high-
yield bonds narrowed over the first half of fiscal 2025; despite widening at the beginning of April, 
when market sentiment deteriorated, they subsequently began to narrow in line with the 
improvement in market sentiment (left panel of Chart II-1-3). Looking at the distribution of credit 
spreads on U.S. high-yield bonds, the overall level of spreads remained low, although spreads on 
some of these bonds remained wide due to the cumulative effects of the high interest rate 
environment (middle panel of Chart II-1-3). Meanwhile, the default rates of both high-yield bonds 
and leveraged loans, which had risen, mainly reflecting the cumulative effects of the high interest 
rate environment, remained more or less flat from the start of 2025 (right panel of Chart II-1-3). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Emerging markets and international commodity markets 
In emerging markets, stock prices rose substantially over the first half of fiscal 2025, moving 
generally in tandem with U.S. stock prices. Currencies in emerging markets appreciated amid the 
trend in the dollar's depreciation, reflecting such factors as uncertainty surrounding the future policy 
conduct of the U.S. administration (Chart II-1-4). In this situation, looking at net flows of emerging 
market funds, both bond funds and equity funds saw net outflows in April when market sentiment 
became cautious; however, they subsequently experienced sustained net inflows, with fluctuations 
smoothed out. 
In international commodity markets, prices of crude oil declined at the beginning of April, due to 
concerns that trade policy in each jurisdiction could cause a global economic slowdown (Chart II-
1-5). Although prices of crude oil temporarily increased thereafter due mainly to concerns over 
geopolitical risks in the Middle East, they declined over the first half of fiscal 2025, driven by weak 
U.S. economic indicators and an increase in production by oil-producing economies.

With regard to term interest rates, the 3-month overnight index swap rate rose slightly over the first 
half of fiscal 2025, as expectations of a policy interest rate hike by the Bank grew (right panel of 
Chart II-2-1). Meanwhile, yields on 3-month T-bills increased slightly, albeit with fluctuations due to 
demand from domestic and foreign investors. 
Japanese government bond (JGB) markets 
Long-term interest rates increased over the first half of fiscal 2025; they declined significantly at the 
beginning of April, due mainly to declining expectations of a policy interest rate hike by the Bank, 
reflecting heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction; however, rates 
subsequently increased against the background of a rise in interest rates in the United States and 
Europe due to the improvement in market sentiment, as well as growing expectations of a policy 
interest rate hike by the Bank reflecting the agreement in tariff negotiations between Japan and the 
United States and other factors (Chart II-2-2). The yield curve for JGBs steepened, driven by a rise 
in super-long-term yields, as attention was paid to fiscal expansion globally. In the meantime, the 
implied volatility of JGB futures continued to be at a high level (Chart II-1-1). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Liquidity and functioning of JGB markets 
The liquidity and functioning of JGB markets continued to improve, following a significant decline 
at the beginning of April. 2 Among liquidity indicators in JGB markets,  bid-ask spreads of newly 
issued bonds and market resiliency in the JGB futures market deteriorated at the beginning of April, 
reflecting a decline in market participants' risk tolerance. They subsequently began to recover in 
line with the improvement in market sentiment (Charts II-2-3 and II-2-4). According to the Bank's 
Bond Market Survey , the diffusion index for the degree of bond market functioning, despite 
remaining negative, also showed an improvement in the August survey, after a significant decline 
within negative territory in the May survey. This development is consistent with the trends in liquidity 
indicators (Chart II-2-5). The reduction of the Bank's purchase amount of JGBs from August 2024 
likely led to enhanced market functioning through an improvement in liquidity, mainly of newly 
issued bonds.

C. Risks to financial markets 
Uncertainty about financial markets remains high. Specifically, attention has been drawn to 
uncertainties over how trade and other policies in each jurisdiction will evolve and how economic 
activity and prices at home and abroad will react to them. Market participants have also paid 
attention to geopolitical risks, developments in major foreign high-tech stocks, and the course of 
fiscal policy in each jurisdiction. 
In stock markets, amid continued high uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction, 
attention is warranted to the risks that market sentiment will deteriorate again due to concerns over 
a global economic slowdown, and that interest rates will remain elevated, driven by a reacceleration 
in inflation in the United States. In addition, there has also been vigilance against the risk of price 
adjustments for major foreign high-tech stocks that have recently experienced rapid price increases. 
In bond markets, market participants have focused their attention on the future conduct of monetary 
policy and developments in fiscal policy in each jurisdiction . In credit markets, as the cumulative 
effects of the high-interest rate environment remain in the United States and Europe, the risk of 
deterioration in financial conditions of firms with low credit ratings and those with high leverage 
ratios, particularly if economic activity decelerates, continues to draw attention. In the U.S. and 
European real estate industries, attention has continued to be paid to developments in commercial 
real estate, mainly reflecting elevated vacancy rates for office buildings. 
In emerging markets, there have been concerns over the risk that capital outflows from countries 
with fiscal and financial vulnerability could occur, with attention continuing to be paid to the 
possibility that trade policy in each jurisdiction will put downward pressure on the economy, mainly 
through global trade developments. In international commodity markets, geopolitical factors and 
uncertainty over developments in the Chinese economy, which have a significant impact on 
commodity and grain prices, warrant attention. 
Attention should continue to be paid to the possibility that the materialization of these risks could 
lead to tightening in global financial conditions through such factors as sharp repricing of risky 
assets and a deterioration in the dollar funding environment.

III. Financial intermediation 
 Financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly in Japan. Despite the increase 
in domestic lending rates, firms' demand for loans has continued to rise mainly on the back 
of economic recovery and developments in mergers and acquisition (M&A) deals. Banks' 
lending stance has also been active. As for foreign lending, major banks have been selective 
amid concerns over uncertainty regarding future developments in foreign economies. 
Meanwhile, banks have been cautious about making securities investment amid concerns 
over the risk of higher interest rates in Japan. 
 Assets under management held by non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) in Japan have 
remained on an uptrend. Investment funds' assets under management have remained on 
an increasing trend on the back of inflows of funds from households. An increase in financial 
dealers and brokers' short-term repo transactions has continued on both the asset and 
liability sides. Life insurance companies' accumulation of holdings of super-long-term 
Japanese government bonds (JGBs) has reached a plateau as they have mostly finished 
making adjustments to comply with new regulations. 
A. Financial intermediation by the banking sector 
1. Loans 
The annual growth rate of domestic loans by privately-owned banks has been at around 3.5 percent 
(Chart III-1-1). In addition to an increase in loan demand reflecting M&A deals and demand for real 
estate-related loans, demand for working capital amid the recovery in economic activity has been 
rising. Downward pressure stemming from repayments on effectively interest-free and unsecured 
loans (so-called zero-zero loans) on the outstanding amount of loans by regional and shinkin banks 
has been abating. Loans to both large and medium-sized firms and small firms have continued to 
increase (Chart III-1-2).

B. Financial intermediation by the NBFI sector

With regard to life insurance companies' valuation gains/losses on securities investment as of the 
end of June 2025, their securities holdings overall have continued to register substantial net 
valuation gains (Chart III-2-3). Although life insurance companies' valuation losses on yen-
denominated bondholdings have continued to increase, reflecting the continued rise in domestic 
interest rates, particularly in the super-long-term zone, their valuation gains on stockholdings have 
remained at high levels on the back of rising stock prices. 5 They have also been able to make 
valuation gains on foreign bondholdings on a yen basis.  As for foreign bond positions, while life 
insurance companies have reduced their holdings of currency-hedged foreign bonds, some of them 
have also shown a cautious stance with regard to accumulating unhedged foreign bonds; the 
outstanding amount of foreign bondholdings has been more or less unchanged (Chart III-2-4). 
The Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF), which is responsible for managing the assets 
of public pension funds such as employees' pension funds and the national pension fund, has been 
rebalancing its portfolio (Chart III-2-5). 6 This is in line with the basic portfolio allocation, which 
determines the fund's portfolio share of each asset class from the perspective of safe and efficient 
asset management over a long-term investment horizon. Corporate pension funds have maintained 
their cautious investment stance without depending on leverage, with many of them having secured 
net assets in excess of policy reserves.

Although the increasing trend in financial dealers and brokers' positions has stalled, short-term

IV. Risks faced by financial institutions 
 The quality of banks' domestic and foreign loan portfolios has been maintained. Even in a 
situation where uncertainties regarding trade and other policies in each jurisdiction have 
remained high, credit costs have been limited so far. With corporate profits in Japan having 
been on an improving trend on the whole, corporate bankruptcies have been more or less 
unchanged, despite some fluctuations. The quality of banks' foreign loan portfolios has 
continued to be maintained as banks have been selective in their foreign lending. 
 Banks have maintained a cautious investment stance, particularly toward investment in yen-
denominated bonds, and their securities portfolios show that overall interest rate risk has 
generally been unchanged for major banks, while it has been on a slight downtrend for 
regional and shinkin banks. Given that banks carry various risk factors, they need to 
continue to adequately manage market risks.  
 Banks have sufficient yen funding liquidity, which mainly consists of small retail deposits. As 
for foreign currency, they have maintained stable funding by using a combination of medium- 
and long-term market funding and the acquisition of sticky corporate deposits. With 
customer channels becoming more digitalized and households' asset choices undergoing 
changes, banks need to continue to work toward establishing stable funding bases, while 
paying attention to changes in the funding environment.

Examining loans by borrower classification, the shares of "normal" loans have stayed high, and the 
shares of borrowers classified as "in danger of bankruptcy" and below have remained at historically 
low levels (Chart IV-1-2). The quality of banks' domestic and foreign loan portfolios has been 
maintained.

IV. Risks faced by financial institutions 
A. Credit risk 
27 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Since April 2025, no major changes have been seen in corporate bankruptcies and defaults, and 
credit costs have been limited so far, even in a situation where uncertainties regarding trade and 
other policies in each jurisdiction have remained high. Looking into how market participants factor 
in the impact of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction on large Japanese firms, 
expected default frequencies (EDFs), derived from market variables including stock prices, rose 
temporarily after the announcement of reciprocal tariffs in April 2025, mainly in automobile and 
electrical machinery industries; however, as agreements on tariffs were reached subsequently, 
they have largely returned to levels comparable to the 2024 average (Chart IV-1-3). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Given that the effect of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction will likely materialize 
gradually, careful monitoring continues to be warranted on whether the quality of banks' loan 
portfolios will change. This chapter first describes recent developments in bankruptcies and then 
examines future risks based on firms' financial positions.

1. Domestic credit risk 
Developments in corporate bankruptcies and defaults 
Corporate bankruptcies have been more or less unchanged, albeit with fluctuations (Chart IV-1-4). 
The upward trend in indicators of default rates since the pandemic has stabilized somewhat. The 
ratio of operating profits to sales for large manufacturing firms declined in the second quarter of 
2025, mainly due to the effects of the appreciation of the yen and the rise in tariffs, but remains at 
a high level. Corporate profits are on an improving trend overall (left panel of Chart IV-1-5). Under 
these circumstances, the proportion of financially vulnerable firms among small and medium-sized 
enterprises (SMEs), such as firms that are either making operating losses with negative net worth 
or are making operating losses, has been falling, likely contributing to the stabilization in the 
increase in corporate bankruptcies and defaults  (middle panel of Chart IV-1-5). However, the 
distribution of the ratio of operating profits to sales for SMEs, which widened during the pandemic, 
has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels, and there are a considerable number of firms whose 
profit recovery has been more moderate than the overall trend (right panel of Chart IV-1-5). For 
these firms, in particular, rises in raw material prices, labor shortages, and rising labor costs may 
be adding further pressure.8 Furthermore, bankruptcies and defaults, which were held in check by 
the measures to support corporate financing implemented during the pandemic, may continue to 
occur with a delay, particularly among financially vulnerable firms. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
8 As pointed out in the previous Report, it is important to note that there is considerable heterogeneity in firms' 
financial soundness across industries, as the proportion of firms that are making operating losses with negative net 
worth is particularly high in the food services and accommodation industry.

will be directly affected by the decline in trade volume. In terms of credit extended to industries 
forecasting a decline in profits, both major banks and regional  banks have relatively modest 
exposures to these industries in their corporate loan portfolios.

fragmentos_texto.texto: Not to be released until 3:00 p.m. Japan Standard Time on Thursday, October 23, 2025. (English translation prepared by the Bank's staff based on the Japanese original) Financial System Report October 2025

The total of major banks, regional banks, and shinkin banks covered in this Report is as follows (as of end-September 2025). Major banks comprise the following 10 banks: Mizuho Bank, MUFG Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, Resona Bank, Saitama Resona Bank, Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Corporation, Mizuho Trust and Banking Company, Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, SBI Shinsei Bank, and Aozora Bank. Regional banks comprise the 61 member banks of the Regional Banks Association of Japan (regional banks I) and the 36 member banks of the Second Association of Regional Banks (regional banks II). Shinkin banks are the 247 shinkin banks that hold current accounts at the Bank of Japan. This Report basically uses data available as of end-September 2025. Please contact the Financial System and Bank Examination Department at the e-mail address below to request permission in advance when reproducing or copying the contents of this Report for commercial purposes. Please credit the source when quoting, reproducing, or copying the contents of this Report for non-commercial purposes. Financial System Research Division, Financial System and Bank Examination Department, Bank of Japan post.bsd1@boj.or.jp

i Objectives of the Financial System Report The Bank of Japan's Financial System Report has two main objectives. The first is to assess the stability of Japan's financial system. The second is to communicate with all related parties on the future tasks and challenges in order to ensure the system's stability. The Report assesses the vulnerabilities of the financial system from a macroprudential perspective. Within a macroprudential framework, institutional designs and policy measures are developed based on risk assessments in the financial system in order to ensure the stability of the overall financial system. In so doing, the interconnectedness of the real economy, financial markets, and financial institutions' behavior are taken into account. The Bank uses the results of the analysis set out in the Report in planning policies to ensure the stability of the financial system and for providing guidance and advice to financial institutions through on-site examinations and off-site monitoring. It makes use of the results in international discussions on regulation, supervision, and vulnerability assessment. In relation to the conduct of monetary policy, the macro assessment of financial system stability is also regarded as important input for the Bank in assessing risks in economic and price developments from a medium- to long- term perspective. Motivations behind the October 2025 issue At the beginning of April 2025, asset prices fluctuated significantly in global financial markets due to heightened uncertainties regarding trade policies in each jurisdiction. Currently, uncertainties remain high regarding the formulation of economic policies in each jurisdiction, and regarding geopolitical risks and developments in global financial markets. This Report analyzes the following four points. First, this Report analyzes the effects of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction on domestic corporate sector and banks' credit costs. As a result of changes in trade and other policies

in each jurisdiction triggered by, for example, the materialization of geopolitical risks, global trade volume could fall substantially, adversely affecting corporate profits. This Report also provides an analysis of the resilience of the financial system if such tail risks were to materialize. Second, with regard to stock and real estate prices, the transaction environment in each market is examined, thereby providing an analysis of potential future risks. Third, this Report explores the possibility that foreign non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs), such as hedge funds, which have been increasing their presence both domestically and internationally, may have an effect on Japanese financial markets, particularly through the rapid unwinding of investment positions. Fourth, this Report provides updates on the effects of changes in the interest rate environment on banks, households, and firms. With regard to developments in deposits, this Report examines the effects of structural factors such as demographic changes and the spread of digital channels, and those of other factors that affect bank deposits amid rising interest rates.

I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system 1 I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system Japan's financial system has been maintaining stability on the whole. In the loan market, financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly as firms' demand for loans has continued to rise and banks' lending stance has remained active. Under such circumstances, no major financial imbalances have been seen in current financial activities. Japanese banks have sufficient capital bases and stable funding bases to withstand significant stresses, including those equivalent to the global financial crisis that would cause major corrections in financial markets and the real economy at home and abroad, as well as those with compound factors particularly resulting from the materialization of geopolitical risks that would cause a substantial decline in global trade volume, and lead to global increases in inflation and interest rates. However, uncertainties remain high regarding the formulation of economic policies in each jurisdiction, and regarding geopolitical risks, and developments in global financial markets. Financial institutions need to be vigilant against the materialization of various risks. From a long- term perspective, if structural factors remain, such as a decline in firms' loan demand reflecting the shrinking population and other factors, banks' profitability and loss-absorbing capacity could decline, depending on the supply and demand balance in the loan market, and this could lead to a contraction of financial intermediation activities or an overheating, such as excessive search for yield. From the perspective of maintaining stability in Japan's financial system, close attention is warranted on future developments in the financial system, while examining both overheating and contraction risks (Chart I-1). Developments in asset prices  Chapters II, IV-B, and V-A In global financial markets, at the beginning of April, stock prices fell substantially as market sentiment became significantly cautious, reflecting

the heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction. Since then, prices of risky assets have risen, with market sentiment improving, reflecting factors such as progress in trade negotiations. The heat map shows that stock prices has been "red," which signals an upward deviation from the trend (Chart I-1). In terms of stock valuations as of the end of September, price-earnings (P/E) ratios remain generally at historical average levels while risk premiums indicated by the equity yield spreads, i.e., the difference between expected equity yields and 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yields, have declined somewhat (left panel of Chart I-2). Given that uncertainties regarding the formulation of trade and other economic policies in each jurisdiction remain high, sentiment in global financial markets could become cautious. Given that Japanese banks have a certain amount of market risk associated with stockholdings, close attention should be paid to developments in risky asset prices, including stock prices. In addition, robust property demand supported by a moderately recovering economy, coupled with demand for investments, including condominium transactions and commercial real estate purchases by foreign investors, also likely contributes to this trend. I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system 3 basis, foreign investors, including hedge funds, have increased transaction volume in JGB markets significantly (Chart I-4). Hedge funds have been increasing their leverage, primarily through repo financing. In the event of unexpected changes in market environment, hedge funds' rapid position adjustments accompanied by deleveraging can amplify volatility in asset prices. If such adjustments occur in government bond markets, this could affect a wide range of financial instruments in Japan. It is necessary that banks manage their risks associated with securities holdings while paying attention to the possibility of investment activities by the foreign NBFI sector causing stress in domestic financial markets. Corporate bankruptcies and defaults and the effects of trade and other policies in each jurisdiction  Chapters IV-A and VI-B Amid the continuing moderate economic recovery, corporate profits in Japan have been improving on the whole, and the proportion of firms that are either making operating losses with negative net worth or are making operating losses, which increased during the pandemic, has been falling. Corporate bankruptcies and defaults have been more or less unchanged, albeit with fluctuations (Chart I-5). However, it is necessary to bear in mind that labor shortages, rising labor costs and rises in raw material prices may be adding further pressure. Japan's corporate sector appears to be reasonably resilient to the effects of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction. The profit projections released by large firms reveal that, given that their financial positions leading up to the current stress are favorable, large firms' debt repayment capacity seems to be maintained overall despite the effects of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction (left panel of Chart I-6). As for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the effects on their profits and default

rates are likely limited overall, as many SMEs have ample on-hand liquidity (middle and right panels of Chart I-6). However, if the stress caused by changes in trade and other policies turns out to have a larger impact on profits than assumed in the projections, debt repayment capacity could deteriorate significantly among firms whose financial positions are relatively vulnerable, including small and medium-sized supplier firms. In exporting industries, the proportion of large loans tends to be high; therefore, attention is also warranted to the fact that if individual firms were downgraded, the impact on credit costs could be significant. Banks need to make various assumptions regarding such structural factors and market fluctuations, and also manage their portfolios appropriately, taking into account their loss-absorbing capacity. Meanwhile, with regard to banks' deposits, the year-on-year growth rate in deposits from both individuals and firms has remained positive; however, the pace of increase has decelerated recently (Chart I-8). While financial assets held by households continue to increase overall and investments in stocks and stock investment trusts have increased, the rate of increase in households' deposits has recently slowed. By type of bank, the share of regional and shinkin banks in total deposits has remained on a declining trend, and most recently there has been a shift from demand deposits to time deposits. The effect on developments in deposits of structural factors such as demographic changes and the spread of digital channels needs attention, and the impact on interest rate risk of changes in the composition of deposits also needs attention. The Bank will promote financial institutions' initiatives to address these potential vulnerabilities through on-site examinations and off-site monitoring. From a macroprudential perspective, it will continue to closely monitor the impact on the financial system of various risk-taking activities by financial institutions. Financial System Report October 2025 6 II. Risks observed in financial and capital markets  Looking at developments during the first half of fiscal 2025, stock prices fell substantially and credit spreads on corporate bonds widened in global financial markets at the beginning of April, as market sentiment became significantly cautious, reflecting heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction. Thereafter, however, prices of risky assets rose, with market sentiment improving, reflecting factors such as progress in trade negotiations.1  In Japanese financial markets, stock prices fell substantially at the beginning of April, mainly due to the effects of increasingly cautious market sentiment in global financial markets. Thereafter, they increased significantly reflecting the agreement in tariff negotiations between Japan and the United States, while following the recovery in U.S. stock prices. Long-term interest rates rose over the first half of fiscal 2025, albeit with fluctuations reflecting progress in trade negotiations and changes in market participants' views on the future conduct of monetary policy by the Bank of Japan.  Uncertainty about financial markets remains high. Specifically, attention has been drawn to uncertainties over how trade and other policies in each jurisdiction will evolve and how economic activity and prices at home and abroad will react to them. Market participants have also paid attention to geopolitical risks, developments in major foreign high-tech stocks, and the course of fiscal policy in each jurisdiction. In this situation, attention should continue to be paid to the possibility that global financial conditions could tighten through such factors as sharp repricing of risky assets and a deterioration in the dollar funding environment. Global financial markets during the first half of fiscal 2025 Looking at developments during the first half of fiscal 2025, stock prices fell substantially and credit spreads on corporate bonds widened in global

financial markets at the beginning of April, as market sentiment became significantly cautious, reflecting heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction. Thereafter, however, prices of risky assets rose, with market sentiment improving, reflecting factors such as progress in trade negotiations. U.S. and European bond markets U.S. long-term interest rates were more or less flat over the first half of fiscal 2025 (Chart II-1-1). They declined at the beginning of April amid a deterioration in market sentiment, reflecting heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction. Thereafter, although they temporarily rose with the improvement in market sentiment owing to progress in trade negotiations, they became more or less flat as expectations of policy interest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve heightened in response to weak U.S. economic indicators. The yield curve for U.S. Treasuries steepened in reflection of such factors as growing expectations of policy interest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve and concerns over a deterioration in supply and demand conditions in U.S. Treasuries due to expansionary fiscal policy. European long-term interest rates were more or less flat over the first half of fiscal 2025. They decreased at the beginning of April in tandem with U.S. interest rates. Financial System Report October 2025 8 U.S. and European credit markets In U.S. and European credit markets, credit spreads on both investment-grade bonds and high- yield bonds narrowed over the first half of fiscal 2025; despite widening at the beginning of April, when market sentiment deteriorated, they subsequently began to narrow in line with the improvement in market sentiment (left panel of Chart II-1-3). Emerging markets and international commodity markets In emerging markets, stock prices rose substantially over the first half of fiscal 2025, moving generally in tandem with U.S. stock prices. In this situation, looking at net flows of emerging market funds, both bond funds and equity funds saw net outflows in April when market sentiment became cautious; however, they subsequently experienced sustained net inflows, with fluctuations smoothed out. Financial System Report October 2025 10 With regard to term interest rates, the 3-month overnight index swap rate rose slightly over the first half of fiscal 2025, as expectations of a policy interest rate hike by the Bank grew (right panel of Chart II-2-1). Meanwhile, yields on 3-month T-bills increased slightly, albeit with fluctuations due to demand from domestic and foreign investors. Japanese government bond (JGB) markets Long-term interest rates increased over the first half of fiscal 2025; they declined significantly at the beginning of April, due mainly to declining expectations of a policy interest rate hike by the Bank, reflecting heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction; however, rates subsequently increased against the background of a rise in interest rates in the United States and Europe due to the improvement in market sentiment, as well as growing expectations of a policy interest rate hike by the Bank reflecting the agreement in tariff negotiations between Japan and the United States and other factors (Chart II-2-2). The yield curve for JGBs steepened, driven by a rise in super-long-term yields, as attention was paid to fiscal expansion globally. In the meantime, the implied volatility of JGB futures continued to be at a high level (Chart II-1-1). Liquidity and functioning of JGB markets The liquidity and functioning of JGB markets continued to improve, following a significant decline at the beginning of April. 2 Among liquidity indicators in JGB markets, bid-ask spreads of newly issued bonds and market resiliency in the JGB futures market deteriorated at the beginning of April, reflecting a decline in market participants' risk tolerance. despite remaining negative, also showed an improvement in the August survey, after a significant decline within negative territory in the May survey. Financial System Report October 2025 14 C. Risks to financial markets Uncertainty about financial markets remains high. Specifically, attention has been drawn to uncertainties over how trade and other policies in each jurisdiction will evolve and how economic activity and prices at home and abroad will react to them. Market participants have also paid attention to geopolitical risks, developments in major foreign high-tech stocks, and the course of fiscal policy in each jurisdiction. In stock markets, amid continued high uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction, attention is warranted to the risks that market sentiment will deteriorate again due to concerns over a global economic slowdown, and that interest rates will remain elevated, driven by a reacceleration in inflation in the United States. In addition, there has also been vigilance against the risk of price adjustments for major foreign high-tech stocks that have recently experienced rapid price increases. In bond markets, market participants have focused their attention on the future conduct of monetary policy and developments in fiscal policy in each jurisdiction . In credit markets, as the cumulative effects of the high-interest rate environment remain in the United States and Europe, the risk of deterioration in financial conditions of firms with low credit ratings and those with high leverage ratios, particularly if economic activity decelerates, continues to draw attention. In the U.S. and European real estate industries, attention has continued to be paid to developments in commercial real estate, mainly reflecting elevated vacancy rates for office buildings. In emerging markets, there have been concerns over the risk that capital outflows from countries with fiscal and financial vulnerability could occur, with attention continuing to be paid to the possibility that trade policy in each jurisdiction will put downward pressure on the economy, mainly through global trade developments. In international commodity

markets, geopolitical factors and uncertainty over developments in the Chinese economy, which have a significant impact on commodity and grain prices, warrant attention. Attention should continue to be paid to the possibility that the materialization of these risks could lead to tightening in global financial conditions through such factors as sharp repricing of risky assets and a deterioration in the dollar funding environment. III. Financial intermediation A. Financial intermediation by the banking sector 15 III. Financial intermediation  Financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly in Japan. Despite the increase in domestic lending rates, firms' demand for loans has continued to rise mainly on the back of economic recovery and developments in mergers and acquisition (M&A) deals. Banks' lending stance has also been active. As for foreign lending, major banks have been selective amid concerns over uncertainty regarding future developments in foreign economies. Meanwhile, banks have been cautious about making securities investment amid concerns over the risk of higher interest rates in Japan.  Assets under management held by non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) in Japan have remained on an uptrend. Investment funds' assets under management have remained on an increasing trend on the back of inflows of funds from households. An increase in financial dealers and brokers' short-term repo transactions has continued on both the asset and liability sides. Life insurance companies' accumulation of holdings of super-long-term Japanese government bonds (JGBs) has reached a plateau as they have mostly finished making adjustments to comply with new regulations. In addition to an increase in loan demand reflecting M&A deals and demand for real estate-related loans, demand for working capital amid the recovery in economic activity has been rising. Downward pressure stemming from repayments on effectively interest-free and unsecured loans (so-called zero-zero loans) on the outstanding amount of loans by regional and shinkin banks has been abating. Financial intermediation by the NBFI sector 21 interest rate fluctuations, and others have accumulated holdings of foreign bonds in anticipation of future policy interest rate cuts, with all aiming to obtain capital gains. Strategic stockholdings, i.e., stockholdings for the purpose of maintaining business ties with firms, have continued to fall, partly as a response to growing social awareness regarding corporate governance. Regional and shinkin banks have been cautious toward increasing their holdings of yen- denominated bonds, led by regional banks, amid concerns over the risk of higher interest rates. Both regional and shinkin banks have shortened the duration of their yen-denominated bondholdings by holding back investments in the longer-term zone. Some of them have sold their securities with low investment yields. Meanwhile, regional and shinkin banks' foreign bond holdings have remained more or less unchanged. III. Financial intermediation B. Financial intermediation by the NBFI sector 23 With regard to life insurance companies' valuation gains/losses on securities investment as of the end of June 2025, their securities holdings overall have continued to register substantial net valuation gains (Chart III-2-3). Although life insurance companies' valuation losses on yen- denominated bondholdings have continued to increase, reflecting the continued rise in domestic interest rates, particularly in the super-long-term zone, their valuation gains on stockholdings have remained at high levels on the back of rising stock prices. 5 They have also been able to make valuation gains on foreign bondholdings on a yen basis. As for foreign bond positions, while life insurance companies have reduced their holdings of currency-hedged foreign bonds, some of them have also shown a cautious stance with regard to accumulating unhedged foreign bonds; the outstanding amount of foreign bondholdings has been more or less unchanged (Chart III-2-4). Financial System Report October 2025 26 IV. Risks faced by financial institutions  The quality of banks' domestic and foreign loan portfolios has been maintained. Even in a situation where uncertainties regarding trade and other policies in each jurisdiction have remained high, credit costs have been limited so far. With corporate profits in Japan having been on an improving trend on the whole, corporate bankruptcies have been more or less unchanged, despite some fluctuations. The quality of banks' foreign loan portfolios has continued to be maintained as banks have been selective in their foreign lending.  Banks have maintained a cautious investment stance, particularly toward investment in yen- denominated bonds, and their securities portfolios show that overall interest rate risk has generally been unchanged for major banks, while it has been on a slight downtrend for regional and shinkin banks. Given that banks carry various risk factors, they need to continue to adequately manage market risks.  Banks have sufficient yen funding liquidity, which mainly consists of small retail deposits. As for foreign currency, they have maintained stable funding by using a combination of medium- and long-term market funding and the acquisition of sticky corporate deposits. With customer channels becoming more digitalized and households' asset choices undergoing changes, banks need to continue to work toward establishing stable funding bases, while paying attention to changes in the funding environment. IV. Risks faced by financial institutions A. Credit risk 27 Since April 2025, no major changes have been seen in corporate bankruptcies and defaults, and credit costs have been limited so far, even in a situation where uncertainties regarding trade and other policies in each jurisdiction have remained high. Looking into how market participants factor in the impact of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction on large Japanese firms, expected default frequencies (EDFs), derived from market variables including stock prices, rose temporarily after the announcement of reciprocal tariffs in April 2025, mainly in automobile and electrical machinery industries; however, as agreements on tariffs were reached subsequently, they have largely returned to levels comparable to the 2024 average (Chart IV-1-3). Financial System Report October 2025 28 1. Domestic credit risk Developments in corporate bankruptcies and defaults Corporate bankruptcies have been more or less unchanged, albeit with fluctuations (Chart IV-1-4). The upward trend in indicators of default rates since the pandemic has stabilized somewhat. The ratio of operating profits to sales for large manufacturing firms declined in the second quarter of 2025, mainly due to the effects of the appreciation of the yen and the rise in tariffs, but remains at a high level. Corporate profits are on an improving trend overall (left panel of Chart IV-1-5). Under these circumstances, the proportion of financially vulnerable firms among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), such as firms that are either making operating losses with negative net worth or are making operating losses, has been falling, likely contributing to the stabilization in the increase in corporate bankruptcies and defaults (middle panel of Chart IV-1-5). However, the distribution of the ratio of operating profits to sales for SMEs, which widened during the pandemic, has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels, and there are a considerable number of firms whose profit recovery has been more moderate than the overall trend (right panel of Chart IV-1-5). For these firms, in particular, rises in raw material prices, labor shortages, and rising labor costs may be adding further pressure.8 Furthermore, bankruptcies and defaults, which were held in check by the measures to support corporate financing implemented during the pandemic, may continue to occur with a delay, particularly among financially vulnerable firms. 8 As pointed out in the previous Report, it is important to note that there is considerable heterogeneity in firms' financial soundness across industries, as the proportion of firms that are making operating losses with negative net worth is particularly high in the food services and accommodation industry.

Financial System Report October 2025 34 Next, as a stress case that takes the uncertainty regarding projected profits due to developments in trade volume into account, (3) a stress is assumed whereby large manufacturing firms' profits come in far below projections. This stress case subtracts two standard deviations of the historical difference between projected and actual profits from the SME profits under scenario (2) which assumes a larger effect on SMEs than scenario (1) (case 3 in Chart IV-1-11). The results show that the share of SMEs in the intermediate goods and parts manufacturing industries with an ICR below 1 rises quite substantially as a result of large firms' profits falling short of their projections. Although default probabilities also rise, the increase is small -- about 0.1 percentage points at the median -- reflecting firms' sound financial conditions, such as ample on-hand liquidity, prior to the stress event. However, given the large heterogeneity in firms' financial conditions, for those SMEs with strong downward pressure on their profits, there is a risk that default probabilities may rise as a result of diminishing on-hand liquidity and rising leverage to offset the decline in liquidity. Given the high degree of uncertainty surrounding the future direction of trade policies and their impact on the real economy, continued vigilance is warranted. Firms' resilience to rising interest rates Finally, firms' resilience to higher interest rates is examined. As summarized in the previous Report, the number of firms in the economy as a whole whose borrowings exceeding their cash and deposit holdings (firms whose interest-bearing debt exceeds their holdings of cash and deposits) is decreasing, and even among firms whose borrowings exceeding their cash and deposit holdings, the overall ICR has risen (Chart IV-1-12). Calculating the change in default probabilities if interest rates were to be mechanically

raised, and ignoring the downward pressure on default probabilities caused by the economic recovery, shows that, similar to the assessment in the previous Report, the increase overall in the probability of default for firms whose borrowings exceeding their cash and deposit holdings would be limited; however, firms with high leverage or insufficient on-hand liquidity tend to be more sensitive to higher interest rates. Thus, credit management of loans to financially vulnerable firms continues to warrant attention. IV. Risks faced by financial institutions A. Credit risk 35 2. Foreign credit risk As of the end of fiscal 2024, Japanese banks' foreign credit risk has remained low (Chart IV-1-13). Non-performing loan (NPL) ratios and credit cost ratios have declined, affected by improvements among some large borrowers in the United States. Although loan-loss provision ratios have declined as a result of the aforementioned developments in large borrowers, loan-loss provision ratios have been at relatively high levels, partly due to forward-looking loan-loss provisioning, including for the effects of trade and other policies in each jurisdiction. The break-even credit cost ratio of banks' international business (net interest income on foreign loans/foreign loans outstanding) remains relatively high, and even if considerable credit costs were to be incurred, they could be absorbed by net interest income. The composition of foreign loans' credit ratings by type of product shows that the quality of banks' foreign loan portfolios has been maintained on the whole (Chart IV-1-14). Investment grade loans have continued to account for almost 70 percent of corporate loans overall. The rating composition of leveraged loans, which entail relatively high risk, has improved slightly due to a leveling-off in downgrades reflecting the effects of past interest rate increases. Turning to the rating composition of project finance loans, the share of investment grade loans has declined as banks have been selective in their lending based on profitability.
